newsitem.title: FRANCE: French EU deficit forecast no surprise - economist.
newsitem.headline: French EU deficit forecast no surprise - economist.

text.p: Economists said on Wednesday they were not surprised by a European Commission forecast that France's 1997 public deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product would be three percent but said the outcome was still uncertain.

They said it was difficult to give an accurate assessement of the forecast as there was no indication whether the French government had promised further spending cuts or simply assured the Commission it would do whatever it takes to hit the target.

They also said the May/June parliamentary election in France added a further element of uncertainty as the opposition Socialists have said they would not introduce any tough fiscal measures even if they were needed to meet the goal.
The French finance ministry was not immediately available for comment.

"It will depend strongly on the outcome of the election first, and besides the outcome of the election, the three percent seems, in our view, slightly optimistic," Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris said. "But we don't know all the components they've used, for example, the dollar forecast."

"I'm not surprised by France," Valerie Plagnol, economist at Credit Commercial de France said. "But we don't know what the basis of the calculation is as the member states provide the numbers. We do know there will have been some arbitrage, perhaps with governments saying they will do whatever is necessary."
She said it was not obvious from the forecasts whether France had promised to cut spending further if the centre-right coalition wins a parliamentary election.

The Commission forecasts were released on the same day a report in a Portuguese newspaper said the International Monetary Fund was forecasting the French deficit at 3.3 percent in 1997 and 3.4 percent in 1998.

Another French economist at a French bank, who asked not to be quoted by name, said while the IMF forecast may well be more accurate from an economic point of view at the moment, the Commission prediction was probably more relevant for markets.
"The Commission is political and European so you'd better rely on this one. The truth on the economic side, however, is more with the IMF," he said.

"But what should the markets look at? They have to concentrate on what the Commission says, it will be choosing the countries that join EMU in May 1998. Whether you believe the forecast or not is a different question," he said.

Mange said, "Regarding France, if nothing is done the IMF forecasts could be correct. There have to be some special measures taken to reduce the deficit (in 1997) and that's partly why the election was called."

He said 3.3 would be more realistic if the Socialists win, but the eventual outcome could well be lower if the centre-right coalition, which has said it is committed to hitting three percent, retains its majority.
